en: The Jātaka:
The Section of Eleven, Chapter on the Supporter of His Mother.
3. The Dhammadevaputta Jātaka:
“I am one who brings glory and performs merit;
I am always praised by recluses and brahmins.”
“I am the Dhamma, worthy of the path, honored by gods and men;
give me the way of unrighteousness!
“Having mounted the firm vehicle of unrighteousness...”
“I am not non-existent, I am powerful;
for what reason would I give you today the path of Dhamma that has never been given before?”
“Indeed, Dhamma appeared first;
afterwards, Adhamma arose in the world.
Dhamma is the eldest, the best, and the eternal.”
“Depart from the path, younger brother, for the elder.
“I would not give you the path even through begging, nor by a fitting request, nor because I am worthy of it.”
“Let there be a battle between us both today;
whoever wins in this battle, his shall be the path.
“I have spread throughout all directions.”
Possessing great power and immeasurable fame,
incomparable and endowed with every excellence—
how could you, O Dhamma, ever defeat Adhamma?
Gold is indeed struck by iron,
but iron is not struck by gold;
if unrighteousness were to strike righteousness today, [it would be a great wonder].
You are as beautiful to behold as fine gold.
But if you are powerful in war and unrighteous,
then neither your elders nor your teachers exist for you.
“I give you the path through both the pleasant and the unpleasant, and I forgive you for the harsh words you have spoken.
Having heard these words, [he thought: “This is unrighteousness...”
Falling headlong with feet upwards:
"If one who seeks battle does not obtain battle," to this extent is it that unrighteousness is slain.
Having conquered the army of battle with the power of patience,
having struck down unrighteousness and crushed it upon the earth, he,
being joyful, mounted his chariot and set forth.
One who is exceedingly strong through the Path alone and diligent in truth—
yet whose mother, father, recluses,
and brahmins have not been honored in his own home.
Having cast off this very body right here,
at the breaking up of the physical frame, they go to hell,
just as unrighteousness falls headlong.
For one by whom mother, father, and ascetics and brahmins have been well-honored in their own home—
having cast off this physical body right here—
At the breaking up of the body, they go to a happy destination,
just as one who has mounted a chariot drawn by the Dhamma.
Thus ends the third Jātaka, the Dhammadevaputta-jātaka.
